Building Tables by Hand

Source: vignettes/articles/summarize.qmd 
library(apa7)
library(flextable)
library(ftExtra)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(tidyr)
library(stringr)
set_flextable_defaults(
  theme_fun = theme_apa,
  font.family = "Open Sans",
  text.align = "center",
  table_align = "left"
)
apa7_defaults(font_family = "Open Sans", line_spacing = 1.5)

Summarizing by Hand

Functions that automate your descriptive statistics tables for you (e.g., the amazing gtsummary package) inevitably entail some level of compromise. It is unreasonable for a single function to anticipate the diversity of needs out there. Sometimes you need a table to be a particular way, and you need to do the heaving lifting yourself. After all that, the apa_flextable function will get a flextable table close to APA style. You may need to do some additional styling with flextable as well.

The flextable package helper functions for automating summary tables. The tabulator, summarizor, and proc_freq functions are particularly powerful ways of summarizing and describing data. However, I am going to compute my summaries with standard base R and tidyverse functions. Here I create a table of means, standard deviations, and sample sizes for several variables across groups. The particulars are not so important here, just that apa7 and flextable can do most of the rest after that.

The bfi data set in the psychTools package (Revelle, 2019) has the answers of 2,800 people to 25 personality items, along with their education. psych::scoreFast averages the items of each Big Five scale (reversing the reverse-keyed items), and the summaries are computed by education:

bfi_scales <- psych::scoreFast(psychTools::bfi.keys, psychTools::bfi)

d_bfi <- psychTools::bfi |>
  transmute(
    Education = factor(
      education,
      levels = 1:5,
      labels = c("Some high school", 
                 "High school graduate", 
                 "Some college",
                 "College graduate", 
                 "Graduate degree")
    ),
    Conscientiousness = bfi_scales[, "conscientious-A"],
    Neuroticism = bfi_scales[, "neuroticism-A"],
    Openness = bfi_scales[, "openness-A"]
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(Education))

d_summary <- d_bfi |>
  arrange(Education) |>
  pivot_longer(where(is.numeric), names_to = "Variable") |>
  summarise(
    M = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    SD = sd(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = n(),
    .by = c(Variable, Education)) |>
  pivot_longer(c(M, SD)) |>
  unite(Variable, Variable, name) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Variable)

The apa_flextable function handles the formatting automatically. Table 1 decimal aligns all the numbers, though this is apparent in column n only.

apa_flextable(d_summary)

Functions such as apa_parameters and apa_descriptives make finished tables from model objects and data. When no function makes the table you need, apa7 can still do most of the work of turning a data frame of results into an APA-style table. This article shows how, starting with apa_flextable and ending with full control over every step.

From a Data Frame to an APA Table

Suppose we have results we want to put in a table:

d <- tibble(
  Model = paste("Model", c(1, 1, 2, 2, 2)),
  Predictor = c(
    "Constant", "Socioeconomic status",
    "Constant", "Socioeconomic status", "Age"
  ),
  b = c(-4.5, 1.23, -5.1, 1.45, -.23),
  beta = c(NA, .24, NA, .31, .031),
  t = c(-18.457, 2.345, -22.457, 2.114, .854),
  df = c(85, 85, 84, 84, 84),
  p = c(.0001, .0245, .0001, .0341, .544)
)

d
#> # A tibble: 5 × 7
#>   Model   Predictor                b   beta       t    df      p
#>   <chr>   <chr>                <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 Model 1 Constant             -4.5  NA     -18.5      85 0.0001
#> 2 Model 1 Socioeconomic status  1.23  0.24    2.35     85 0.0245
#> 3 Model 2 Constant             -5.1  NA     -22.5      84 0.0001
#> 4 Model 2 Socioeconomic status  1.45  0.31    2.11     84 0.0341
#> 5 Model 2 Age                  -0.23  0.031   0.854    84 0.544

With the flextable package’s APA theme (set in the setup chunk with set_flextable_defaults), flextable gets us close:

flextable(d)

Getting from “close” to “exactly right” requires a series of polishing steps:

  • Make Model into row titles (Model 1, Model 2).
  • Left-align and widen the Predictor column.
  • Use true minus signs (−) instead of hyphens.
  • Align numbers on their decimals.
  • Format p-values, and drop the leading zeros of beta and p.
  • Italicize statistical symbols in the headers (e.g., b → b).

The flextable package has functions for each of these, but applying them by hand is tedious. As a general-purpose package, flextable should not be expected to know the rules of a particular style guide. The apa_flextable function applies them all:

apa_flextable(d, row_title_column = Model)

Rows and Groups

Row titles can be aligned to the left, center, or right:

apa_flextable(d, row_title_column = Model, row_title_align = "center")

Without row titles, groups can be shown with a vertically merged column instead:

d |>
  mutate(Model = str_remove(Model, "Model ")) |>
  apa_flextable() |>
  merge_v() |>
  align(j = "Predictor", part = "all") |>
  align(j = "Model", align = "center") |>
  valign(j = "Model", valign = "middle") |>
  surround(i = 2, border.bottom = flextable::fp_border_default()) |>
  width(width = c(.8, 1.75, rep(.8, 5)))

Columns and Headers

Column spanners and deckered heads

The apa_flextable function treats underscores in column names as header levels: in Openness_M, “Openness” is a column spanner (a label over several columns) and “M” is a deckered head (the label of one column under it). Here are the means and standard deviations of the personality scales from above, by education, without the sample sizes:

d_personality <- d_summary |>
  select(-n)

d_personality
#> # A tibble: 5 × 7
#>   Education            Conscientiousness_M Conscientiousness_SD Neuroticism_M
#>   <fct>                              <dbl>                <dbl>         <dbl>
#> 1 Some high school                    4.12                0.941          3.26
#> 2 High school graduate                4.23                0.985          3.23
#> 3 Some college                        4.39                0.908          3.13
#> 4 College graduate                    4.22                0.941          3.06
#> 5 Graduate degree                     4.28                0.980          3.06
#> # ℹ 3 more variables: Neuroticism_SD <dbl>, Openness_M <dbl>, Openness_SD <dbl>
apa_flextable(d_personality)

separate_headers = FALSE turns this off. column_spanner_label adds the same spanner to several columns, selected by name or with tidyselect functions such as starts_with. The selected columns are moved next to the first one (relocate = FALSE keeps them in place):

d |>
  column_spanner_label("Significance test", c(t, df, p)) |>
  column_spanner_label("Coefficients", starts_with("b")) |>
  apa_flextable(row_title_column = Model)

Tables of cell statistics

pivot_wider_name_first is like tidyr::pivot_wider, but it puts the names first (e.g., High_M rather than M_High), so the new columns get a spanner for each name. This makes tables of cell statistics in a factorial design easy to build. In the Moore data set in the carData package (Moore & Krupat, 1971), participants made judgments with a partner of low or high status, and the number of times they conformed to their partner’s judgments was recorded. Their authoritarianism was classified as low, medium, or high. Here are the mean, standard deviation, and size of each cell, with a row for each partner status and a spanner for each level of authoritarianism:

d_cells <- carData::Moore |>
  transmute(
    `Partner Status` = factor(partner.status,
                              levels = c("low", "high"),
                              labels = c("Low", "High")),
    Authoritarianism = factor(fcategory,
                              levels = c("low", "medium", "high"),
                              labels = c("Low", "Medium", "High")),
    Conformity = conformity
  ) |>
  summarise(
    M = mean(Conformity),
    SD = sd(Conformity),
    n = n(),
    .by = c(`Partner Status`, Authoritarianism)
  ) |>
  arrange(`Partner Status`, Authoritarianism)

d_cells
#>   Partner Status Authoritarianism        M       SD  n
#> 1            Low              Low  8.90000 2.643651 10
#> 2            Low           Medium  7.25000 3.947573  4
#> 3            Low             High 12.62500 7.347254  8
#> 4           High              Low 17.40000 4.505552  5
#> 5           High           Medium 14.27273 3.951985 11
#> 6           High             High 11.85714 3.933979  7
d_cells |>
  pivot_wider_name_first(
    names_from = Authoritarianism,
    values_from = c(M, SD, n)
  ) |>
  apa_flextable()

The spanners follow the order in which the levels first appear in the data, so sort the data first. There is another example in A Complete Custom Table below. To count the cells of a contingency table instead, use apa_chisq (see the contingency tables article). The flextable package can also place statistics into cells: tabulator arranges precomputed statistics by row and column variables, and proc_freq makes frequency tables with row, column, and total percentages. Their output can be styled with apa_style.

Break columns

By default, a narrow blank column separates groups of columns under different spanners. add_break_columns inserts break columns yourself, after any column selected by name or with a tidyselect function:

d_personality |>
  add_break_columns(ends_with("SD"), omit_last = TRUE) |>
  apa_flextable()

apa_flextable treats any column whose name begins with apa7breakcolumn as a break column.

Formatting Values

Decimal alignment

align_chr rounds numbers (to .01 by default), replaces hyphens with true minus signs, and pads numbers with figure spaces on both sides of the decimal so that all values in a column have the same width:

tibble(x = align_chr(c(2.431, -0.4, -10, 101))) |>
  apa_flextable(table_width = .2) |>
  align(align = "center")

Trailing zeros can be dropped, and leading zeros can be trimmed (for statistics such as correlations that cannot exceed 1):

tibble(x = align_chr(c(2.431, -0.4, -10, 101),
                     drop0trailing = TRUE,
                     trim_leading_zeros = TRUE)) |>
  apa_flextable(table_width = .2) |>
  align(align = "center")

Stars

add_star_column adds significance stars in a column of their own, so the numbers stay aligned. The column to the left of the stars is right-aligned, and the stars are left-aligned:

d_star <- tibble(
  Predictor = c("Constant", "Socioeconomic status"),
  b = c(.45, .55),
  p = c(.02, .0002)
) |>
  add_star_column(b, p = p)

apa_flextable(d_star)

If stars are already appended to numbers, separate_star_column moves them into a column of their own:

tibble(
  Predictor = c("Constant", "Socioeconomic status"),
  b = c("1.10***", "2.32*"),
  beta = c(NA, .34)
) |>
  separate_star_column(b) |>
  apa_flextable()

p2stars converts p-values to stars, and apa_p_star_note writes the note that explains them.

Hanging indents and numbered lists

flextable has no hanging indent, so hanging_indent wraps text and indents the continuation lines with figure spaces:

d_quote <- tibble(
  Quote = c(
    "Believe those who are seeking the truth. Doubt those who find it.",
    "Resentment is like drinking poison and waiting for the other person to die.",
    "Advice is what we ask for when we already know the answer but wish we didn’t.",
    "Do not ask whether a statement is true until you know what it means.",
    "Tact is the art of making a point without making an enemy.",
    "Short cuts make long delays.",
    "There is a stubbornness about me that never can bear to be frightened at the will of others. My courage always rises at every attempt to intimidate me.",
    "There is a crack in everything, that’s how the light gets in."
  ),
  Attribution = c(
    "André Gide",
    "Carrie Fisher",
    "Erica Jong",
    "Errett Bishop",
    "Howard W. Newton",
    "J. R. R. Tolkien",
    "Jane Austen",
    "Leonard Cohen"
  )
) |>
  arrange(nchar(Quote))

d_quote |>
  mutate(Quote = hanging_indent(Quote, width = 55, indent = 5)) |>
  apa_flextable() |>
  align(j = "Attribution", part = "all") |>
  width(width = c(4.5, 2))

add_list_column numbers the rows. Set type to "A", "a", "I", or "i" for letters or Roman numerals:

d_quote |>
  add_list_column(Quote, type = "A", sep = ") ") |>
  apa_flextable() |>
  align(j = "Attribution", part = "all") |>
  width(width = c(.3, 4.5, 1.7))

Automatic Column Formatting

apa_flextable formats the columns and headers it recognizes (e.g., b, beta, t, df, and p). To turn this off:

apa_flextable(d, row_title_column = Model, auto_format_columns = FALSE)

Each recognized column has a column_format: its header (in markdown), its LaTeX header, a function that formats its values, and an optional definition for table notes. To change how a column is shown, make a new format. Here, any column named Predictor is relabeled “Variable” and shown in capitals:

cf_predictor <- column_format(
  name = "Predictor",
  header = "Variable",
  latex = "Variable",
  formatter = stringr::str_to_upper
)

column_formats makes the full set of default formats, which can be changed. Here, numbers are rounded to .001, the new Predictor format is added, and beta is no longer formatted:

my_formats <- column_formats(accuracy = .001)
my_formats$Predictor <- cf_predictor
my_formats$beta <- NULL

apa_flextable(d, row_title_column = Model, column_formats = my_formats)

To use the formats in every table, set them with apa7_defaults(column_formats = my_formats). These are the default formats:

column_formats()@get_tibble |>
  select(-formatter) |>
  arrange(name, .locale = "en") |>
  apa_flextable(markdown_body = FALSE)

Changing a Finished Table

apa_flextable returns a flextable, so any flextable function can change it afterward. For example, to bold one cell:

apa_flextable(d, row_title_column = Model) |>
  bold(i = 3, j = 3)

These flextable functions solve common formatting problems. Each can be applied to selected rows (including rows chosen by a condition on the data) and columns:

A Complete Custom Table

Here the unstandardized and standardized coefficients of the two models are side by side, with stars appended to the unstandardized coefficients and a note below the table:

d |>
  # Decimal-align b and append stars
  mutate(b = paste0(align_chr(b), p2stars(p))) |>
  select(-c(t, df, p)) |>
  # One column for each statistic in each model
  pivot_wider_name_first(names_from = Model, values_from = c(b, beta)) |>
  apa_flextable() |>
  add_footer_lines(
    values = as_paragraph_md(
      c(
        paste(
          "*Note*. *b* = unstandardized regression coefficient.",
          "&beta; = standardized regression coefficient."
        ),
        apa_p_star_note()
      )
    )
  ) |>
  align(part = "footer", align = "left")

Inside apa_flextable

The apa_flextable function does more than might be apparent at first glance. To understand what it does under the hood, I have outlined the major steps in changing a data frame into a flextable in APA format. With a few minor details omitted, it does roughly this:

  1. Adds a break column between adjacent column spanners, if add_breaks_between_spanners = TRUE and separate_headers = TRUE. A break column is a narrow blank column without borders, so the rules under adjacent spanners do not touch.
  2. If auto_format_columns = TRUE, turns columns of whole numbers (e.g., degrees of freedom) into integers so that they have no decimals. Then formats the columns with apa_format_columns, Columns named in no_format_columns, or in a "no_format_columns" attribute of the data (set by functions such as apa_loadings), are left as they are.
  3. Makes the flextable. With row_title_column, it first restructures the data with flextable::as_grouped_data, and each row title gets a rule above it (row_title_border).
  4. Separates the headers into spanners and deckered heads, if separate_headers = TRUE.
  5. Left-aligns the first column and centers the columns of numbers.
  6. Applies apa_style to style the table and convert markdown.
  7. Aligns the row titles (row_title_align) and indents the rows under them.
  8. Sets the column widths with pretty_widths.
  9. Lines up numbers padded by align_chr on their decimal points.
  10. Draws a rule above the rows named in a "rule_above" attribute of the data (set by functions such as apa_loadings and apa_chisq).
  11. Adds the note, if note is given. It is added last so that a long note does not widen the columns.

Most of these steps can also be applied one at a time. Here they are with column spanners added for illustration (steps 9 through 11 are not included, because they use functions inside apa7):

d |>
  # Column spanners
  rename_with(.cols = c(b, beta), \(x) paste0("Coefficients_", x)) |>
  rename_with(.cols = c(t, df, p), \(x) paste0("Significance Test_", x)) |>
  # Step 1: Space between column spanners
  add_break_columns(ends_with("beta")) |>
  # Step 2: Whole numbers as integers, then format the columns
  mutate(across(where(rlang::is_integerish), as.integer)) |>
  apa_format_columns() |>
  # Step 3: Row titles and the flextable
  flextable::as_grouped_data("Model") |>
  mutate(row_title = Model, .before = 1) |>
  fill(Model) %>%
  flextable(col_keys = colnames(select(., -Model, -row_title))) |>
  mk_par(i = ~ !is.na(row_title), value = as_paragraph(row_title)) |>
  merge_h(i = ~ !is.na(row_title)) |>
  surround(
    i = ~ !is.na(row_title),
    border.top = list(color = "gray20", style = "solid", width = 1)
  ) |>
  # Step 4: Spanners and deckered heads
  flextable::separate_header() |>
  # Step 5: Alignment
  align(j = 1, part = "all") |>
  # Step 6: Style the table and convert markdown
  apa_style() |>
  # Step 7: Row titles centered, other rows left-aligned
  align(j = 1, i = ~ is.na(row_title)) |>
  align(i = ~ !is.na(row_title), align = "center") |>
  # Step 8: Column widths
  pretty_widths()

Speed

By default, apa_flextable converts markdown in every cell (with ftExtra::colformat_md). This makes formatting easy and consistent, but it is a little slow, and a document with many tables can take a while to render. markdown_body = FALSE skips the conversion in the body of a table whose cells have no markdown, and caching the chunks of finished tables (with the cache chunk option) avoids remaking them each time the document is rendered.

References

Moore, J. C., & Krupat, E. (1971). Relationship between source status, authoritarianism, and conformity in a social influence setting. Sociometry, 34(1), 122–134. https://doi.org/10.2307/2786355
Revelle, W. (2019). psychTools: Tools to accompany the psych package for psychological research (Version 2.6.4) [Computer software]. Comprehensive R Archive Network. https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.psychTools
